The Orange-breasted sunbird Anthobaphes violacea is a striking nectarivore endemic to the fynbos of South Africa. Recorded life history traits for this species originate from field studies in the Western Cape and observations of captive individuals. Neonates emerge from the egg at a very modest size, with the wet weight at birth being just 1.2 grams [Wwb = 1.2 grams]. The initial weight of a newly laid egg, representing the mass of the ovum prior to substantial embryonic development, has been documented at 1.29 grams [Ww0 = 1.29 grams], indicating a relatively small investment per offspring at the moment of oviposition. These tiny values underscore the altricial nature of the nestling, which requires intensive parental brooding and provisioning. In terms of reproductive output, females produce 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], and typically approximately 1.7 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.7 clutches each year], a pattern consistent with a slow life-history pace among small passerines.

Eggs are incubated for a period that appears to be temperature-dependent. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to first exogenous feeding, averages 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days]. This value falls comfortably within the observed natural range of 11 to 16 days (11-16 days) [ab = 11-16 days] reported from nest monitoring in the wild at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The relatively short incubation period is typical for small passerines and may be an adaptation to reduce exposure of the clutch to predators in the open fynbos vegetation. Following hatching, the nestling period is characterized by rapid mass gain driven by frequent provisioning of nectar and small arthropods by the adult female. The brood is entirely dependent on the female for warmth and food during the early days of life, and the synchrony of hatching is usually tight within a given clutch.

Under an ambient temperature regime typical of the active metabolic season, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental milestones of the nestling are tightly linked. The time since birth at fledging, marking the achievement of first flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This milestone is reached relatively quickly for a bird of this body size, reflecting the intense selection pressure to escape the high predation risk of the nest. In contrast, the attainment of sexual maturity is deferred considerably, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 57 days after hatching [tp = 57 days after hatching], suggesting that while the nestling gains independence swiftly, the full maturation of the reproductive system requires several additional weeks of post-fledging growth and foraging experience at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaches 5 years [am = 5 years] under these same thermal conditions, a notable longevity among nectarivorous passerines of similar body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

The ultimate adult body mass shows a clear sexual dimorphism, with males growing to a larger final size than females, a common pattern among sunbirds where males compete for territories. The ultimate wet weight for a fully grown female is 8.8 grams [Wwi = 8.8 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for a mature male reaches 9.7 grams [Wwi = 9.7 grams]. This difference of nearly ten percent in body mass likely reflects the energetic demands of male-male competition and territory defense, as males engage in prolonged aerial displays and chases to secure high-quality feeding territories rich in nectar-producing Protea and Erica species. Females, by contrast, bear the sole responsibility for nest construction and incubation and may therefore be under different selective pressures related to maneuverability and energy economy during the breeding season. The mass of a breeding female, recorded at 8.8 grams [Wwi = 8.8 grams], is a useful benchmark for metabolic studies in this species.

The onset of the first breeding attempt in this species occurs after a full annual cycle of growth and establishment. At the same active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth], meaning that young birds hatched in one breeding season typically do not commence their own reproductive efforts until the following spring. This deferred first reproduction aligns with a relatively extended lifespan for such a small bird. The combination of a low reproductive rate, with only a single clutch per year of 1 to 3 eggs, and a moderate lifespan of up to 5 years suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival in a seasonally variable and sometimes harsh fynbos environment. The species thus exemplifies an equilibrium life-history strategy where adult survivorship is prioritized over high annual fecundity, a common pattern among nectarivorous birds inhabiting resource-poor Mediterranean-type ecosystems.
